project.name: Holiday sneaker drop
project.summary: A one-page flash sale for 100 pairs of limited-edition sneakers at $49.99, one pair per customer. Shoppers sign in, enter a shipping address and press Buy; the sale opens at midnight after an email blast. (This is the worked example in this repository: the demo app's `fixed/` version, after two rounds of review and fixes.)
project.author: The demo team (this repository)
project.riskReason: the app calls the card provider's charge API itself, so amounts, repeat-safety, time-outs and reconciliation are its own job, and the whole sale happens in a promoted 60-second rush.
project.reviewer: Claude Code (launch-review skill), in sessions that hadn't written the code
project.reviewedOn: 2026-10-17; extended 2026-10-27 with checks of the tests, the AI-coding instructions and past problems
project.versionNote: the app's code hasn't changed since; later commits touch only documentation and tests

verdict.reason: Don't launch yet: four things block it. The most serious is that the opening time can silently be wrong, so the sale could open hours early or stay shut at midnight. And the shop has never taken a real card payment: the connections to the real payment provider, sign-in and database aren't built yet. The previous review found 23 problems; 16 are now fixed and verified, and 7 are still open in some form (partly fixed, accepted as a risk, or waiting on a condition). Together with the new problems this review found, the open ones are listed under What to fix.

blockers.text: Make the opening time impossible to set wrong: one place where it's set, only full times with a time zone, and the time in force shown in the admin answer and in the log.
Connect the real database, sign-in and card payment, make production refuse to start without them, have a reviewer check them, then make one small real purchase and refund.
blockers.who: Developer, with the providers you choose; you make the test purchase
blockers.effort: One to two weeks, depending on the providers

blockers.text: Show that backups can be restored, that an alert reaches a named person, and who is on call on launch night.
blockers.who: Hosting provider or developer; you name the on-call person
blockers.effort: About a day, once recovery targets are agreed
blockers.why: Required for a high-risk launch (risk tier 3).

blockers.text: Build the operator tools the launch-night runbook relies on, try each once, and make the way back to the previous version work.
blockers.why: Required for a high-risk launch: without them, problems on the night can't be handled.

conditions.text: Set up a test copy of the shop (staging) with its own database, keys and test payments, so the runbook and the real payment can be rehearsed safely.
Run one copy of the app only, and set the load balancer's idle timeout below 65 seconds.
Start production with a real start command that sets `NODE_ENV=production`.
Repeat the load test on production-sized machines, with the load generator on its own machine.
Add instructions for the AI coding assistant, and tests for bad input and restarts, before the next round of AI-written fixes.
Book an independent security test (penetration test).
conditions.effort: External: typically a few days of a security firm's time

verdict.ifLaunchedNow: The sale might open before the email goes out, letting bots and early visitors take the pairs, or stay shut while 3,000 people wait. Nobody knows whether a real card payment goes through, so the first real customer is the first test. Customers get no confirmation email. If something breaks during the sale, the documented way back (rollback) fails, and nobody is named to be woken up.
noticeable: No confirmation email after buying: emails are queued but never sent (ARC-07).
The sign-in box stays on the page after signing in, and the stock count doesn't change after buying (ARC-15).
The page mentions an order history and an email that don't exist (ARC-14).
If the page goes live more than about 25 days before the sale, it reloads itself non-stop (PERF-04).
Shoppers who sign in early and open a new tab are signed out (OPS-03).

decisions.text: Choose the payment provider, sign-in provider and email provider (or decide to launch without confirmation emails).
Agree how much order data you could afford to lose, and how fast the shop must be back after a failure (for example: at most 5 minutes of orders, back within 30 minutes).
Set the sale date. If the sale page goes live more than 25 days before it, the page reloads itself non-stop until PERF-04 is fixed.
Decide how long a payment may stay "confirming" before the pair goes back on sale and the shopper is told.
Accept, in writing and until a date, running only one copy of the app on launch night.
Decide whether to remove the page's mentions of an order history and an email, or have them built.
Sign this page once the blockers are done.

verdict.estimate: An estimate, not a promise: about two to three weeks of developer work once the providers are chosen, most of it connecting real payments, plus the time to book a security test. Set the sale date after that.

architecture.summary: One Node.js program behind a load balancer, with no framework and no third-party packages. It keeps orders in a database, calls the payment provider directly with one repeat-safe key per order, and runs two background jobs (settling payments whose outcome is unknown, and sending confirmation emails from a queue) plus small housekeeping timers. In this demo a local SQLite file stands in for the hosted Postgres database a real deployment would use, and a simulator stands in for the payment provider.
architecture.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Shopper["Shopper's browser"] -->|HTTPS| LB["Load balancer"]
  Admin["Staff: shared admin token"] -->|HTTPS| LB
  LB --> App["Node.js app (one instance)"]
  App -->|"pool of 10, 1 s wait"| DB[("Postgres: orders, stock, settings, email queue")]
  App -->|"3 s limit, key per order"| Pay["Payment provider"]
  Recon["Reconciler, every 5 s"] --> DB
  Recon -->|"same key"| Pay
  Mailer["Email sender, every 1 s"] --> DB
  Mailer -.->|"not built yet"| Mail["Email provider"]
  IdP["Sign-in provider (not in repo)"] -.-> Shopper

performance.slowPartner: With the payment provider answering in about 3 seconds: 40 charges for 40 paid orders, and 60 for 60 in a second run; repeat clicks were refused. The previous version charged 57 times for 39 pairs.

history.period: Three reviews, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-17, and the git history of `demo/flash-sale/` (10 commits, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-18).
sources: Three review reports on this app: the first version (30 problems), round 1 (23) and round 2 (all 23 re-checked, plus 13 new): `demo/flash-sale/sample-reports/`. Problems are labelled Review 1, 2 and 3 below. Problem codes restart in each review: "Review 1 PERF-03" is not the same problem as PERF-03 under What to fix.

Git history of `demo/flash-sale/`, scanned with `history-scan.mjs`: 10 commits, all with an AI co-author. Five look like fixes, but the two that matter bundle a whole round each (79 and 29 files), so git can't separate individual defects here and the review reports are the defect record.
No issue tracker or incident log exists for the demo.

stats.label: Problems found by the three reviews (before 2026-10-27)
Files in the biggest fix commit

classes.name: Outside calls whose outcome is unknown

occurrences.text: No time limit on the payment call: one slow charge holds the request for 30 s.
A time-out was treated as a failure: 57 charges for 39 pairs. Introduced by the fix for the missing time limit.
Database busy right after payment: the shopper is told "very busy" and the paid order is stuck.
An error that retrying can't fix leaves orders "confirming" forever.

classes.rootCause: Every outside call was modelled as success or failure. "Unknown" (timed out, but the provider may still have charged) wasn't a state, so each fix moved the problem: no time limit, then a time-out treated as failure, then "unknown" with no deadline. The tests' payment stub never completed a charge after the app gave up, so the tests couldn't see it.
classes.control: A realistic payment simulator (finishes abandoned charges, hangs 2% of calls), used by acceptance test AC-08 in CI and by the slow-provider runs.
classes.controlCheck: AC-08 fails on the round-1 code and passes on round 2; slow provider: 40 charges for 40 orders.
classes.agentRule: Every outside call: a time limit, a repeat-safe key, and an explicit "unknown" state settled by the reconciler with the same key, with a deadline.

classes.name: Bad input crashes the app or is quietly accepted

occurrences.text: Malformed JSON crashes the whole site.
A malformed Host header crashes the server.
One `GET //` crashes the shop. Introduced by the fix for the Host header.
A request body of `null` gives a 500 error.
"Nov 27" is accepted as 27 November 2001 and opens the sale.
The address check drops every non-Latin letter, so different addresses collide.

classes.rootCause: Each handler parses its own input with forgiving built-ins (`new URL`, `JSON.parse`, `new Date`, a regular expression), and each fix patched the one input that failed. There is no single validation layer and no test that sends malformed input.
classes.control: Code-scanning rules `url-parse-outside-try` and `json-parse-in-stream-callback`; the reviewer's malformed-path script (7 paths, all answered 400).
classes.controlCheck: The rules' own tests run in CI, but the rules aren't run against the app in CI, and the malformed-input script isn't in the test suite.
classes.agentRule: Parse every input once, strictly, at the edge; refuse rather than guess; add each new input to the malformed-input test.

classes.name: Settings and data that must survive restarts and deploys

occurrences.text: Every start-up recreates the database and deletes all orders.
Settings and secrets live in the code.
Every start still deletes all orders and resets stock.
A one-call "delete every order" endpoint ships to production.
Test sign-in and demo secrets can reach production.
Changing `SALE_STARTS_AT` after the first start does nothing, while the log says it did. Introduced by the round-2 fix.
Rolling back to the previous release fails against the new database. Introduced by the round-2 migrations.

classes.rootCause: Start-up, settings and deploy behaviour was never specified or tested. Every test starts a fresh app on an empty in-memory database, so the second start, start-up with old data, and the previous release were invisible.
classes.control: Versioned migrations; production refuses demo switches and placeholder secrets; the reviewer's restart script with a saved database.
classes.controlCheck: A restart keeps orders (verified in round 2), but no restart or rollback test runs in CI, and ARC-11 and OPS-09 are still open.
classes.agentRule: Any change to start-up, settings or the database needs a test that starts the app twice on the same data, and one that starts the previous release.

classes.name: Business rules checked in code instead of enforced by the database

occurrences.text: Stock is read, then written back: 1,962 pairs sold out of 100.
No one-per-customer limit and no repeat-safety: 963 shoppers charged twice.
No database constraints for any business rule.
The price is taken from the browser.
"One per customer" is really one per email address.
Still easy to get round, and nothing slows bots down.

classes.rootCause: Rules were written as checks inside request handlers, which simultaneous requests and small variations slip past. Once moved into atomic updates and unique indexes they held; the identity behind "one per customer" is still weak.
classes.control: Atomic stock update, unique indexes and `CHECK (stock >= 0)`, with the race test in CI.
classes.controlCheck: Race test in CI on every change: 1,000 buyers, 100 sold, 0 charged twice.
classes.agentRule: Enforce limits with constraints or atomic updates, never check-then-write; the race test must pass.

classes.name: Screen behaviour no test looked at closely

occurrences.text: The page gets stuck when the server is busy or the session has expired.
Pairs returned after a failed payment are never offered again (found by a test).
The sign-in box never disappears; it has been there since the first version.
A countdown longer than about 25 days reloads the page non-stop. Introduced by the round-2 countdown.
The page points to an order history and an email that don't exist.

classes.rootCause: The acceptance tests check what should appear, never what should disappear or change, and nothing tests the page's timers and error paths. The page was reviewed through the server's eyes.
classes.control: Guidance "assert what should disappear, too" added to the acceptance-test skill.
classes.controlCheck: Not applied to this suite yet: no test checks that the sign-in box hides.
classes.agentRule: For every change of state on the page, test what appears and what disappears.

classes.name: Operations promised on paper but not in tools

occurrences.text: No error tracking, uptime monitoring or alerts.
No backups or recovery.
The launch-night safety nets aren't in evidence.
Still listed in the runbook, still not shown.
The runbook relies on tools that don't exist: loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses, comparing charges with orders.

classes.rootCause: Operations were written down as intentions (a runbook, a checklist) but never rehearsed, so missing tools and broken steps stayed invisible until a reviewer tried them.
classes.control: Checklist rule: every runbook step must be backed by a tool that exists and has been tried.
classes.controlCheck: No rehearsal has been run yet.
classes.agentRule: Don't add a runbook step without the command that performs it and a log of it being tried.

areaNotes.R: A reviewer can run the app and its tests from the README in minutes. What's missing is a staging copy and any agreed figure for acceptable data loss and recovery time.
areaNotes.H: The tests that exist check orders, charges and messages, cover payment failures and double clicks, and pass reliably in CI; they don't check what should disappear from the page. What's missing is the layer that keeps the next AI-written change on track: there are no instructions for coding assistants, no test sends malformed input or restarts the app (two problems that came back), and nothing lints or type-checks the server.
areaNotes.A: A deliberately small design: one process, no packages, every decision on the server. It handles slow payments correctly now. The weak points are the opening time, which can be silently wrong, and a rollback that fails.
areaNotes.D: Stock, duplicates and the price are enforced by the database and proven by a 1,000-buyer race. The gaps are input that's accepted when it should be refused (the opening time) and payments that can stay "confirming" forever.
areaNotes.S: Access to orders, injection, secrets and error messages are sound, and test-only routes are refused in production. Still open: a shared admin password, a weak one-per-customer identity with no bot protection, and the production sign-in, which isn't in the code to review.
areaNotes.P: The expected rush passes in every run with a lot of room to spare, the race never oversold, and a slow payment provider no longer causes double charges. Capacity above 150% isn't proven, because everything ran on one laptop-class machine.
areaNotes.O: Health checks, safe restarts and the pause switch work. Backups, alerts, the on-call rota and the runbook's tools haven't been shown, and the documented rollback fails.
areaNotes.Q: The same kinds of problem came back across three reviews, and several problems were introduced by fixes. None is yet caught fully automatically: the counts are in the tiles below.
areaNotes.U: Every agreed criterion passes three runs in a row, with screenshots. The criteria were agreed before testing and re-approved when they changed.

findings.title: The real database, sign-in and card payment aren't connected
findings.impact: The code talks only to stand-ins: a local SQLite file instead of the hosted Postgres database, a test sign-in that accepts any email, and a payment simulator. Card details, 3-D Secure, declines and refunds have never been handled, so the first real customer would be the first test.
findings.who: Developer, with the providers the product owner chooses
findings.where: Database: `shared/db.mjs` (SQLite stand-in). Sign-in: `POST /api/login` test stub. Payment: `fixed/server.mjs:299-310` (calls the simulator).
findings.fix: Connect hosted Postgres, the chosen sign-in provider and the chosen payment provider (including the provider's lookup call and refunds); have a reviewer check them; then make a purchase, a decline and a refund in the provider's test mode, and one small real purchase and refund.
findings.doneWhen: The race test and acceptance tests pass against staging with the real database and the provider's test mode, and the provider's records match the shop's orders for one real purchase and refund.

findings.title: The opening time can silently be wrong
findings.impact: If the opening time is changed after the first start, the server keeps the old one while its log shows the new one, so the sale can open hours early or stay shut at midnight. A date without a time zone, or text like "Nov 27" (read as 2001), opens the sale at once.
findings.fix: One source of truth, only full times with a time zone, and show the time in force in the log and the admin answer. Effort: small.
findings.doneWhen: A test starts the app twice on the same database with a changed opening time and sees the new time in force; "Nov 27", "1" and a date without a time zone are refused; both run in CI.

findings.confidence: Confirmed (found by an independent test review, 2026-10-27)
findings.title: Production starts without a database or payment address, and a restart then loses every order
findings.impact: With no database setting the app keeps orders only in memory, and with no payment address it calls a test address on the same machine; production mode starts anyway. A restart during the sale then erases every paid order while the customers stay charged (reproduced: 0 paid orders, 1 charge).
findings.where: `fixed/server.mjs:70` (database defaults to memory), `:12` (payment address defaults to localhost)
findings.fix: In production, refuse to start without a real database connection and a payment address.
findings.doneWhen: Starting in production mode without either setting fails, and a restart test with production settings keeps every order.

findings.title: A payment that never resolves stays "confirming" forever
findings.impact: A payment error that retrying can't fix keeps the pair reserved indefinitely: the whole stock could be locked with nothing sold. A warning is written to the log after 10 minutes, but nothing yet delivers log warnings to a person.
findings.fix: Look the payment up instead of re-sending it, give "confirming" a deadline, then release the pair and tell the shopper.
findings.doneWhen: A test where the provider keeps failing ends with the pair released and the shopper told, within the agreed deadline.

findings.title: One person can still buy several pairs, and nothing slows bots
findings.impact: A second mailbox or a re-spelt address buys another pair.
findings.fix: Firmer identity for the limit, and a waiting room or bot protection in front of the drop.
findings.doneWhen: A second mailbox or a re-spelt address can't buy a second pair in a test; a bot-protection or waiting-room service is in front of the drop.

findings.title: Production safety depends on one setting nobody sets
findings.impact: Started without `NODE_ENV=production`, the shop runs with demo secrets, test sign-in and the reset route switched on.
findings.fix: Make production the default: refuse to start with demo values unless demo mode is switched on explicitly, so forgetting one setting can't open the shop with demo settings. Add a real production start command.
findings.doneWhen: Starting without `NODE_ENV` and without an explicit demo switch fails.

findings.title: One shared admin password, and no record of who used it
findings.impact: Anyone with the token can open, move or pause the sale, and the log can't say who did.
findings.fix: Personal admin accounts and an audit entry per change.
findings.doneWhen: Each admin signs in personally; every change to the sale is logged with who made it.

findings.title: Rate limits live in one server
findings.impact: A second instance would halve the protection.
findings.fix: Run one instance (runbook), or move limits to a shared store first.
findings.doneWhen: Runbook and hosting settings run exactly one instance, or limits live in a shared store.

findings.title: Confirmation emails are queued but never sent
findings.impact: Shoppers get no confirmation.
findings.fix: Connect the email provider, with retries per email.
findings.who: Developer; product owner chooses the email provider
findings.doneWhen: A test purchase produces a delivered confirmation email from the real provider.

findings.title: One signed-in script can tie up the database
findings.impact: Unlimited signed-in reads can starve checkout during the rush.
findings.fix: Rate-limit signed-in reads (`GET /api/orders/:id`, `GET /api/my-orders`), for example 10 per 10 seconds per account.
findings.doneWhen: A load test with one account hammering reads leaves checkout times within budget.

findings.title: The page reloads non-stop if the sale is more than ~25 days away
findings.impact: Browser timers overflow above about 25 days, so every open page reloads the product non-stop and hammers the server. The sale date isn't set yet: if the page goes live more than 25 days before the sale, this happens from day one.
findings.fix: Cap the countdown timer and re-check periodically.
findings.doneWhen: A page loaded 60 days before opening re-checks no more than once a minute.

findings.title: Signing in early doesn't survive a new tab
findings.impact: Shoppers who sign in before midnight and open a new tab must sign in again during the rush.
findings.fix: Keep the session across tabs (for example in a cookie or `localStorage`), weighing the risk on shared computers.
findings.doneWhen: A shopper signed in early is still signed in in a new tab at midnight.

findings.title: The launch-night safety nets haven't been shown
findings.impact: Backups, error tracking, alerts and on-call are listed in the runbook but not evidenced.
findings.fix: Show a tested restore, a received test alert and the rota.
findings.who: Hosting provider or developer; product owner names the on-call person and agrees recovery targets
findings.doneWhen: A restore log, a received test alert, and the on-call rota are attached to the review.

findings.title: The runbook relies on tools that don't exist
findings.impact: Loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses and comparing charges with orders have no tool.
findings.fix: Build each tool and try it once.
findings.where: `fixed/RUNBOOK.md` steps for loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses and comparing charges with orders
findings.doneWhen: Each runbook step names a command that exists, and a rehearsal log shows each one run once.
dependsOn: INT-01 (comparing charges with orders needs the real provider)
a staging copy to rehearse on

findings.title: Rolling back to the previous release fails
findings.impact: The rollback the runbook prescribes fails at start-up, so the shop stays down when things are already bad.
findings.fix: Make the previous release start against the new schema, or roll forward with a tested fix.
findings.doneWhen: The previous release starts against the current database in a test, or the runbook replaces rollback with a tried roll-forward step.

findings.title: No request ids, and admin actions are anonymous
findings.impact: Harder to trace one shopper's problem.
findings.fix: A request id per request, and admin identity in the log.
findings.doneWhen: Every log line carries a request id; admin actions name the admin.

findings.title: Different non-Latin addresses collide
findings.impact: A shopper with an address in Japanese, Russian or Greek can be refused because of someone else's address.
findings.fix: Normalise with Unicode-aware rules.
findings.doneWhen: Two different addresses in Japanese or Greek can both order in a test.

findings.title: One failing email would block the rest
findings.impact: Once real sending is added, one failing email would block all later ones, and a second app copy would send every email twice.
findings.fix: Retry per email.
findings.doneWhen: A test with one failing email still sends the rest, once each.

findings.title: The page points to things that don't exist
findings.impact: Shoppers are sent to an order history and an email that don't exist.
findings.fix: Remove the mentions of an order history and an email, or build them.
findings.doneWhen: Every link and promise on the page leads somewhere real.

findings.title: The sign-in box never hides, and the stock count is stale after buying
findings.impact: Confusing during a one-minute sale; some shoppers will sign in again.
findings.fix: Fix the CSS rule that overrides `hidden`, and add a test that it disappears.
findings.doneWhen: An acceptance test checks that the sign-in box disappears and the stock count drops after buying.

findings.title: The product cache drops its last good copy when the database is slow
findings.impact: Slow database means slow pages for everyone.
findings.fix: Serve the last good copy while refreshing.
findings.doneWhen: With a slow database, the page is served from the last good copy within budget.

findings.title: Any `?v=` value is cached for a year
findings.impact: A mixed-version deploy can pin old JavaScript.
findings.fix: Cache only the current hash.
findings.doneWhen: Only the current file version is cached for a year; other `?v=` values get a short cache.

findings.title: No instructions for the AI agents that write the code
findings.impact: Every new session of the AI coding assistant starts without the project's rules and lessons, so the problems under Quality history can return. Several problems so far were introduced by fixes.
findings.fix: Add a short AGENTS.md: how to start and test, the seven business rules, where money and secrets are handled, never edit applied migrations, and one rule per recurring problem linked to its test. Effort: small.
findings.doneWhen: `AGENTS.md` exists; every command in it works; it lists the business rules and one rule per recurring problem, each linked to a test.

findings.title: Two recurring problems have no test: bad input and restarts
findings.impact: Bad input that crashed the app or was quietly accepted, and settings or data lost across restarts, came back again and again across three reviews (see the counts under Quality history); each time only a reviewer caught it.
findings.fix: Move the review's malformed-input and restart scripts into the CI suite, and add a lint and type check for the server. Effort: medium.
findings.doneWhen: A malformed-input test and a start-twice test run in CI, and each fails on an earlier broken version.
dependsOn: ARC-11: its start-twice test is half of this

findings.title: No kind of recurring problem is fully caught automatically yet
findings.impact: Each depends, at least partly, on the next reviewer noticing.
findings.fix: For each kind of recurring problem in Quality history, add an automatic check (test, code-scanning rule or database constraint) and prove it catches a past example.
findings.doneWhen: Every kind of recurring problem is marked "caught automatically".
